title: Stream-multiqueue kernel coordination and KV throttle exploratory notes
content:
Purpose and high-level goal:

This note captures exploratory ideas and early microbench notes for a kernel scheduling/fusion approach that treats NVLink/PCIe-connected GPUs as multi-queue producers for paged KV caches. The objective is to reduce tail latency for medium-length sequences (64-1024 tokens) by: 1) coordinating multi-stream kernel launches across NVLink peers, 2) applying fusion only when queue watermarks predict net throughput gains, and 3) dynamically throttling KV page prefetch/eviction to avoid QoS regressions.

Why this direction?
- We've seen solid perf wins from fusion (FlashAttention + fused linear layers) on single-GPU, but performance drops when KV paging and eviction interfere with steady kernel occupancy.
- Many customers run multi-GPU instances with NVLink; cross-GPU streaming and peer-to-peer copies are underutilized in our current allocator and prefetcher.
- The hypothesis: by treating each GPU as a producer queue and adding a small coordination layer that observes queue watermarks and KV paging state, we can avoid over-fusing or over-prefetching that increases latency for short, latency-sensitive requests.

Key concepts and vocabulary (rough):
- producer queue: per-GPU submission queue of ready microbatches (microbatch ~requests grouped by model and token-length bucket).
- coordinator: lightweight host-side actor that watches per-queue occupancy, KV cache page hit ratios, and target latency SLOs to decide fusion thresholds and prefetch budget per GPU.
- fusion threshold (T_fuse): a dynamic parameter indicating minimum microbatch size or combined op token-count to attempt kernel fusion (e.g., FlashAttention + post-attn linear).
- prefetch budget (B_pref): number of KV pages allowed to be in-flight per GPU before coordinator stalls further prefetch requests.

Design sketches

1) Multi-queue submission model
- Maintain N per-GPU submission queues. Each incoming request is enqueued to a queue local to the GPU chosen by smart routing (affinity by model, region, or historical latency).
- Coordinator periodically samples the queues (lightweight: every 200-400us). It computes occupancy percentiles (p50/p95), average token-length, and short-term throughput.
- Use occupancy percentiles to set T_fuse: if p95 occupancy < small threshold and token-length distribution skewed to short sequences, raise T_fuse to avoid fusion overhead. Otherwise lower T_fuse to favor throughput.

2) Fusion-aware kernel scheduler pseudocode (host side):
- while true:
    sample_queues()
    for each GPU g:
        if kv_page_fault_rate(g) > KV_FAULT_HIGH:
            B_pref[g] = max(B_pref[g] - 1, MIN_B)
        else if queue_p50(g) > OCC_HIGH:
            T_fuse[g] = max(T_fuse[g] - DELTA, MIN_T)
        else:
            T_fuse[g] = min(T_fuse[g] + DELTA, MAX_T)
        candidate = try_make_microbatch(g, T_fuse[g])
        if candidate and B_pref[g] > 0:
            submit_fused_kernel(g, candidate)
        else if candidate:
            submit_unfused_kernels(g, candidate)

Notes: the intent is to preferentially submit fused kernels when there is both queue depth and low KV fault pressure. B_pref acts as a simple backpressure to avoid saturating NVLink/PCIe with page requests that would interfere with kernel progress.

3) KV paging integration and throttling
- Track per-GPU inflight KV page requests and average latency of page reads (p2p or PCIe).
- Implement a fast path: if KV page is resident (cache hit) then fused kernel can proceed; otherwise, coordinator can either: a) expand microbatch to hide page latency (only if latency SLO allows), b) switch to unfused path that issues page read(s) earlier and overlaps compute differently, or c) route request to a different GPU with hot pages.
- Heuristic: if expected page read latency > L_high and queue_p95 < Q_low, prefer to route to another GPU with hot pages or to unfused path to avoid blocking fused kernel.

4) NVLink streaming opportunity
- Use peer-to-peer NVLink copies to move hot KV pages proactively between GPUs when coordinator detects upcoming high-demand. This can amortize page transfer cost across multiple requests if timing aligns.
- Practical constraint: NVLink bandwidth is limited and contention-sensitive; coordinator must budget NVLink transfers similarly to B_pref.

Microbench experiments (informal)
- Setup: 2x A100s connected by NVLink, model = 7B transformer, sequence mix: 60% short(<=128), 30% mid(129-512), 10% long(>512).
- Baseline (no fusion control, aggressive prefetch): p50 latency = 18ms, p95 = 220ms, avg throughput = 170 tok/s/GPU. Observed p95 spikes correlated to KV page faults and eviction storms.
- Simple coordinator (static T_fuse=medium, B_pref=4): p50 = 20ms, p95 = 120ms, throughput = 150 tok/s/GPU. Reduced p95 by limiting aggressive prefetch.
- Dynamic T_fuse & B_pref (small DELTA adjustments in sampling loop): p50 = 19ms, p95 = 95ms, throughput = 152 tok/s/GPU. Notable smoothing of p95 under bursty arrivals.

Interpretation: modest throughput tradeoffs for significant tail-latency improvements. The dynamic coordinator avoided pathological prefetch/eviction patterns that caused long stalls.

Implementation concerns and low-level kernel impacts
- Kernel launch overhead: toggling between fused and unfused kernels frequently can increase host-to-device launch overhead. We need to batch launches using CUDA streams and launch coalescing strategies to hide that cost.
- FlashAttention variants: fused FlashAttention kernels gain most when Q/K/V are resident and memory bandwidth for KV is stable. If page faulting is common, fallback kernels that split compute and page reads with explicit cp.async/await usage may be better.
- Register pressure: fusion increases register usage; on older GPUs (Ampere), this can lower SM occupancy. Coordinator should sample occupancy and can set T_fuse to avoid fusion when occupancy drops.

Open questions and risk areas
- Calibration: how to pick sampling frequency and DELTA to avoid oscillations? We might need PID-like control rather than simple hysteresis.
- Measurement noise: queue sampling on host might be stale; need to quantify staleness effect and possibly add device-side counters accessible via lightweight device-to-host aggregation.
- Scheduling fairness: coordinating prefetch across models and customers is tricky — heavy tenants might force prefetch budgeting that hurts small tenants. We need quotas.
- Complexity vs. benefit: coordination adds non-trivial control code and telemetry. Is tail reduction worth increased system complexity? initial microbench says yes for mixed workloads, but more variants needed.

Next steps and experiments to run
- Short-term (1-2 weeks): implement coordinator prototype in host scheduler using existing per-GPU queues (no device counters). Run multi-GPU microbench with synthetic mixes and measure p50/p95 and NVLink traffic.
- Mid-term (3-6 weeks): add device-side telemetry (counters for page faults, inflight p2p bytes) and experiment with PID controller for T_fuse. Add simple tenant-level quotas for prefetch budget.
- Long-term: integrate with rollout/Console metrics, allow customer-configurable latency-vs-cost points that tweak coordinator aggressiveness. Consider moving part of coordinator logic to a small on-device agent (CUDA kernel or persistent thread) for lower-latency decisions.

References and links inside the org:
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/834 (streaming prefetch refactor)
- Ticket: INF-4123 — paging telemetry gaps
- Slack: #serving-runtime thread on 2024-07-09 (notes from perf sync)

Appendix: quick pseudocode for page-aware fused launch sequence

function launch_candidate(gpu, candidate):
  pages = candidate.kv_pages_needed
  if all resident(pages):
    stream = choose_stream(gpu, "fusion")
    launch_fused(stream, candidate.ops)
  else:
    // attempt overlap: prefetch then compute minimal prefix
    prefetch_pages_async(pages)
    prefix = compute_short_prefix(candidate)
    launch_unfused_prefix(prefix) // compute to hide latency
    await_prefetch_completion()
    launch_remaining_fused_or_unfused()

// End of note

Unresolved TODOs (quick):
- Add synthetic generator for page-fault heavy workload to reproduce worst-case p95s.
- Formalize B_pref as both a count and byte budget (NVLink bytes in-flight).
- Explore storing hot-page bitmaps per-GPU and using bloom filters to route to GPU with highest locality.

If useful, I can spin up a small branch with a host-side coordinator prototype and a harness for the synthetic workload. Comments welcome on the heuristics above and on other device-level signals we should expose.
